title: Usage clustering found 5 personas — target onboarding by persona?

scenario.role: You're the product analyst at Ledgerline
scenario.situation: Dev, the head of Product, clustered accounts on active_days_per_week, features_used, and seat_count and got 5 clean groups. He's briefed the onboarding team to build 5 different onboarding tracks — one per "usage persona" — starting next sprint, and wants your sign-off on the segment definitions.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "The clustering found 5 distinct usage personas. Different onboarding for each, matched to how that persona actually uses the product."
scenario.question: Do these 5 clusters represent 5 different ways accounts actually *use* the product — or did the clustering just rediscover account size? Check what's driving cluster membership before 5 onboarding tracks get built.

columns.name: plan
columns.description: starter, team, or business — pricing tier (not used in clustering, for context)

columns.name: active_days_per_week
columns.description: Average number of days per week someone on the account is active (0-7)

columns.name: features_used
columns.description: Count of distinct product features touched in the last 30 days (0-20)

columns.name: seat_count
columns.description: Number of seats on the account

columns.name: naive_cluster
columns.description: Dev's cluster label (0-4) — k-means(k=5) run directly on the raw active_days_per_week/features_used/seat_count columns, no scaling

columns.name: honest_cluster
columns.description: K-means run on the same 3 features after standardizing each to mean 0 / unit variance, with k chosen by silhouette score

guidingQuestions: Profile Dev's 5 clusters (naive_cluster): mean active_days_per_week, features_used, and seat_count in each. Which column actually moves between clusters?
Compare seat_count's range across accounts to active_days_per_week's range. Which one has room to dominate an unscaled distance calculation?
If active_days_per_week is nearly flat across all 5 naive clusters, what is the clustering actually splitting accounts on?
Re-profile using honest_cluster (features standardized first). Does a genuine usage split appear — accounts that are in the product often and touch many features, versus accounts that barely show up?
If the 5 personas are mostly a seat-count split, what should onboarding actually be built around — usage behavior, or company size (which sales already tracks)?
suggestedApproach: Group by naive_cluster and compute the mean of active_days_per_week, features_used, and seat_count per cluster.
Compare raw ranges: seat_count spans roughly 18-617 across cluster means, active_days_per_week spans roughly 3.3-3.8 — barely moves at all.
Name the mechanism: seat_count's huge scale dominates unscaled Euclidean distance, so k-means effectively clusters on account size and treats usage behavior as noise.
Re-profile using honest_cluster (standardized features, k chosen by silhouette); check whether active_days_per_week and features_used now separate meaningfully.

Contrast the two: naive clusters mostly recover seat_count tiers; honest clusters recover a real behavioral split (frequent multi-feature users vs. rarely-active ones) largely independent of account size.

notebook.intro: Five steps: profile the personas, find which feature actually made them, then compare with a clustering that was scaled properly.

cells.title: Profile the personas
cells.explain: Group by naive_cluster and look at the mean of each feature that went into it.
cells.reads: Read down the columns. One of them changes enormously across the personas and the others barely move.

cells.title: Compare the raw ranges
cells.explain: Look at the spread of each feature across cluster means, in the units k-means actually saw.
cells.code:
spread = profile[["active_days_per_week", "features_used", "seat_count"]].agg(["min", "max"]).T
spread["range"] = spread["max"] - spread["min"]
spread["std in data"] = df[["active_days_per_week", "features_used", "seat_count"]].std()
spread.round(2)
cells.reads: seat_count spans hundreds; active_days_per_week spans a fraction of a day. They were never competing on equal terms.

cells.title: Name the mechanism
cells.explain: Unscaled k-means minimises Euclidean distance, so the largest-magnitude feature dominates. Measure how much of each feature's variance each clustering actually accounts for.
cells.code:
def variance_explained(col, labels):
    grand = df[col].mean()
    groups = df.groupby(labels)[col]
    between = (groups.count() * (groups.mean() - grand) ** 2).sum()
    total = ((df[col] - grand) ** 2).sum()
    return between / total

feats = ["active_days_per_week", "features_used", "seat_count"]
shares = pd.DataFrame({
    "naive_cluster explains": [variance_explained(c, df["naive_cluster"]) for c in feats],
    "honest_cluster explains": [variance_explained(c, df["honest_cluster"]) for c in feats],
}, index=feats)
shares.round(3)
cells.reads: The naive clustering explains almost all of seat_count and almost none of the usage columns. It is an account-size split wearing persona labels.

cells.title: Re-profile with the scaled clustering
cells.explain: honest_cluster was built on standardised features. Check whether behaviour separates now.
cells.reads: Now the usage columns move across clusters, and seat_count is no longer the thing doing the sorting.

cells.title: Contrast the two clusterings
cells.explain: Measure how much each clustering separates behaviour versus account size.
cells.reads: The naive clusters recover a size ranking you already had. The scaled ones recover a behavioural split you did not.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Five clusters, cleanly separated by k-means. Dev reads them as five different ways teams use the product, and briefs onboarding to build a track for each.
teachingNote.theTrap: seat_count ranges from a handful of seats to several hundred; active_days_per_week only ranges 0-7 and features_used only 0-20. On raw, unscaled features, Euclidean distance is dominated by whichever column has the biggest numbers — here, seat_count almost entirely decides who lands in which cluster. Profile the 5 naive clusters and active_days_per_week barely moves (3.3 to 3.8 across every cluster) while seat_count ranges from ~18 to ~617 — a more than 30x spread. The clustering isn't finding 5 usage personas; it's finding 5 account-size tiers, which sales already has in the CRM as company size.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Standardize active_days_per_week, features_used, and seat_count before clustering, and a real usage split emerges: one group is active only ~1.6 days/week touching ~3 features (largely dormant accounts), another is active ~5.2 days/week touching ~11 features (genuine power users), with a middle group in between. This honest split shares almost nothing with the seat-based naive clusters and lines up well with the actual underlying usage pattern. Tell Dev: the 5-track onboarding plan is really a 5-tier account-size plan wearing usage-persona language. If onboarding should differ by how people actually use the product, build it off the standardized clustering (or more simply, directly off active_days_per_week and features_used) — not off the naive clusters, which mostly just re-sort accounts by seat count.
howToGetThere: Profile naive_cluster: group by cluster, average active_days_per_week, features_used, seat_count.
Notice active_days_per_week (~3.3-3.8) and features_used (~6.8-8.8) are nearly flat across all 5 naive clusters — only seat_count moves, from ~18 to ~617.
Name the mechanism: seat_count's raw scale dominates unscaled Euclidean distance, so k-means clusters almost entirely on account size.
Standardize all three features to mean 0 / unit variance and re-cluster (or use the pre-computed honest_cluster column); pick k by silhouette score.
Re-profile the honest clusters: active_days_per_week (1.6 vs 5.2) and features_used (3.0 vs 11.0) now clearly separate — a real usage split, largely independent of seat count.

teachingNote.lesson: Distance-based clustering has no concept of which of your columns is "important" — it just minimizes distance in whatever units you hand it, and the biggest-magnitude column wins by default. A feature measured in the hundreds will silently steamroll features measured in single digits, no matter how behaviorally meaningful those smaller features are. Standardize before you cluster, and always profile the resulting clusters against your raw inputs before naming or acting on them — if one unscaled column alone orders your clusters top to bottom, you've re-discovered that column, not found a new segment.
